questions.question: Why does `if (typeof input === "object")` not remove `null` from `input: object | null`?
options: Because typeof does not narrow at all
Because typeof null is "object" in JavaScript
Because null is a subtype of every object
questions.explanation: typeof null returns "object", so null stays in the narrowed type. Add an explicit `!== null` check.

questions.question: In a switch over a discriminated union, what does `const unhandled: never = s;` in the default branch achieve?
options: It throws at runtime if s is null
It converts s to never so the code compiles
It disables type checking for the default branch
It causes a compile error if any union member is not handled by a case
questions.explanation: If every member is handled, s is never in the default branch. Any unhandled member makes the assignment fail, giving an exhaustiveness check.

questions.question: What is the main risk of a custom type predicate like `function isUpi(v: unknown): v is Upi`?
options: The compiler trusts it, so a buggy body leads to wrong types
It cannot be used with filter
It runs only at compile time
questions.explanation: TypeScript does not verify that the body matches the predicate. Even `return true` compiles, so predicates need careful code and tests.

questions.question: How does an assertion function such as `assertIsDefined(v): asserts v is NonNullable<T>` narrow types?
options: It returns a boolean you must check with if
It narrows only inside the function body
If it returns without throwing, the argument is narrowed for the rest of the scope
It changes the variable's declared type everywhere in the program
questions.explanation: Assertion functions throw on failure. If execution continues past the call, TypeScript narrows the argument for the code that follows.
